# Crank no start - no spark

A crank-no-start condition where there is absolutely no spark, even when you've confirmed power is reaching the ignition coil, narrows the diagnosis down to a specific subset of the ignition system. You have already performed some excellent initial isolation steps: verifying 12V at the coil terminals while cranking and ruling out the spark plugs themselves by placing a new plug on the engine block with no result. This effectively tells us that the high-voltage output path is dead, but not necessarily why.

The resistance measurement you took is a critical data point here. On your 1999 Nissan Micra K12 (the 1.3 gasoline engine), the ignition coil uses an internal resistor to limit current and manage heat. The reading of roughly 12 kOhms is within the expected ballpark for this specific era of automotive electronics, where coils often sit between 8 kOhms and 15 kOhms depending on the exact trim and market specifications.

You noted that your new coil reads 12.4 kOhms after a brief moment where the reading fluctuates. That fluctuation is normal behavior for digital multimeters measuring resistance in live circuits or due to thermal effects, but once it stabilizes at 12.4 kOhms against an original of 11.9 kOhms, your coil is likely perfectly fine. A healthy ignition coil should show a relatively stable resistance that doesn't drift significantly over a few seconds unless the meter lead connection is poor or the component is heating up rapidly. If both coils are reading within 0.5 kOhms of each other, you can safely discard the coil as the primary suspect.

Since you have confirmed 12V at the input leads and zero output spark, the failure point lies in the control logic or the high-voltage switch that actually triggers the discharge. In this specific engine architecture, the ignition system is typically controlled by the Engine Control Unit (ECU) via a signal to an internal transistor or an external ignition module located near the distributor.

Before dismantling the distributor or attempting to replace the coilâa procedure that involves removing the upper intake manifold and often requires specialized toolsâyou must verify the ECU's ability to generate the trigger pulse. The most direct way to do this without full disassembly is to check for a 12V reference signal from the ECU to the ignition module. If you can locate the wiring diagram for your specific K12 chassis code, look for the "IGF" (Ignition Failure) or "CKP" (Crankshaft Position Sensor) circuits.

If the crankshaft position sensor is failing, the ECU will not ground the ignition coil's primary circuit to create a spark, even if power is present at the input terminals. This is a common pitfall: assuming that because the coil has battery voltage, it *should* be sparking. It won't unless the ECU sends the grounding signal.

Additionally, ensure the distributor cap is not internally shorted or cracked in a way that bleeds off the high voltage before it can jump the gap. While you tested with a wire on the block, try placing the tester directly on one of the spark plug wires inside the cap to rule out a catastrophic internal breakdown within the plastic housing itself.

If your multimeter has a continuity or diode test mode, check the ignition module (the component sitting on top of or inside the distributor) for open circuits relative to ground. If the ECU is sending a pulse and power is present at the coil input, but there is still no spark, the internal switching transistor within the module or the ECU itself may have failed.

Replacing the coil in a 1999 Micra is indeed a significant mechanical undertaking involving the removal of the intake manifold gasket and often the throttle body. If your resistance checks pass and the wiring harness continuity to the ignition module is confirmed, proceeding with the coil replacement might only delay finding the actual fault if the trigger signal is missing or if the distributor cap is compromised.

For deeper diagnostics on ECU-driven ignition systems, resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) can sometimes provide community discussions regarding specific engine codes and wiring schematics that differ from generic repair manuals. However, your primary focus should remain on verifying the crankshaft position sensor signal and the integrity of the distributor cap before committing to the labor-intensive coil swap.
